#375. How Playstation nailed its iconic startup screen

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (819 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq

How Playstation nailed its iconic startup screen

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s a short ritual that plays out every time someone switches on a PlayStation.
  • It has been revealed that for more than thirty years, every generation of PlayStation has opened with its own version of this sequence.
  • That intent goes back to the beginning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s a short ritual that plays out every time someone switches on a PlayStation. You press the power button and, before the dashboard appears, movement and sound take over, building through a sequence before the console hands you over to play. It lasts only seconds, but those seconds have a beginning, a build, a pause and a release. They are designed as an experience in their own right.

It has been revealed that for more than thirty years, every generation of PlayStation has opened with its own version of this sequence. The motion, visual language and sound have changed but the decision to design that transition has remained. What could easily be functional downtime has instead become part of the PlayStation experience. It rivals the best motion in logo design, but it also has its own function as well.

That intent goes back to the beginning. When Manabu Sakamoto designed the original PlayStation logo, he wanted it to capture one of the console’s defining promises: 3D. The interlocking P and S created a sense of depth and space rather than simply sitting flat on a 2D screen. By spring 1994, that identity had been turned into an animation, handed to sound designer Takafumi Fujisawa as what the team called a “motion logo.”.

Fujisawa was given little direction beyond that animation and had to set the tone himself, working within tight technical limits. He wanted the startup to feel like walking into a cinema. That particular hush where you sense something is about to begin.

According to recent reports, A straight cut from power-on to interface would give you a change of state and nothing else. Motion gives those few seconds structure; sound and visual design give them character. They are all working together, but motion is what determines how the experience unfolds through time.

Sources indicate that the startup’s primary job isn’t just to create an ‘atmosphere’, as it also helps organise the experience of entering the console itself. The sequence tells the player that something is happening, creates a sense of progression, and makes the eventual handoff into play feel deliberate.

On the original PlayStation, it took on a more practical role. The startup sound helped confirm that the hardware was running correctly and that the disc had been read. If it hadn’t, part of the sound was designed to loop to signal that something was wrong.

The important point is that the startup was not simply decoration sitting on top of a technical process. Motion, sound and visual design were part of how that process was communicated and felt.

That is where motion becomes especially useful. It can signal change, control pace, create anticipation and prepare someone for what comes next.

Sources indicate that over time, the original function of that startup changed. Hardware changed, interfaces changed, and the need to tell a player that a disc had been successfully read stopped mattering. Yet, PlayStation kept designing the transition.

Sources indicate that five generations on, those startups have looked, moved and sounded very different. What has survived through that time is the expectation that switching on any PlayStation from PS1 to PS5 deserves an authored beginning.

Sources indicate that that consistency does not always come from repeating the same expression. It sometimes (and in this case) comes from recognising which moments are the most valuable. PlayStation could change the way those seconds looked and felt because the thing it had established beforehand went beyond the mere execution of it.

Industry observers note that brands spend enormous amounts of time designing the things people see, whether it be the best logos, typefaces, colours, layouts or interfaces. But experiences are also full of moments between those things.

When an app opens, or a payment completes, an audience waits for something to begin. These transitions are easy to treat as functional gaps, especially when the instinct is to get people to the next thing as swiftly as possible. The point, though, is not to add friction; it is to recognise that these moments already exist, and that repeated transitions can become part of the brand experience when they are deliberately designed.

Motion matters disproportionately in those spaces because it works in the same material the moment is made of: time. It determines how one state becomes another, and how that change is experienced along the way. PlayStation was able to make that transition worth designing and returning to in its own right.

Sources indicate that andrew Vucko merges a lifelong interest in motion and design with a passion for brand building. As the founder of Vucko, he leads a global motion studio that transforms brands like Google, Meta, and Spotify through award-winning motion identities, systems, and guidelines.

#374. The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2435 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED

The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government's chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.
  • When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.
  • And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government's chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.

When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.

And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.

“Ten years ago, it would have gone to all of them,” indicates Mark Thomas, a former EPA official who for years managed the airborne detection effort.

Recent findings suggest that the program, known as ASPECT, was designed to respond around the clock to emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills, and radiation. The plane’s sensors could identify chemicals in the air within minutes, giving emergency responders crucial information about the dangers nearby communities face.

For more than two decades, the plane has flown over many of the country’s worst disasters, from New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina to the deadly West Fertilizer explosion in Texas to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

But since early 2021, the single-engine Cessna has responded to just seven emergencies. And former ASPECT scientists say two of those missions—the 2023 train derailment that sent toxic clouds over East Palestine, Ohio, and the 2025 fire at Smitty’s Supply in Louisiana—were badly mismanaged.

It has been revealed that at Smitty’s, the EPA declared the air safe, but a former ASPECT scientist later found toxic chemicals the agency had missed. And the agency’s inspector general is now auditing the response to the East Palestine derailment, including the data behind its public assurances about air quality.

It has been revealed that in June, the EPA inspector general found a more fundamental problem: The plane could no longer identify chemicals within minutes, as designed. Instead, the data had to be analyzed by hand, a process that takes about a week. That’s far too long to help anyone on the ground who’s deciding whether to evacuate.

The EPA mentioned the plane's chemical sensors are wearing out and expects replacements to be working by mid-2027.

Industry observers note that but five people who helped build and run the program told Floodlight that the EPA is fixing the wrong problem. The old sensors still work, they say. What the agency lost, in their view, is the initiative and expertise that made the program a powerful tool when disaster struck. Replacing the old sensors, they warn, could leave the EPA even less capable of detecting hazardous chemicals in an emergency.

“I fear that the public is at risk,” claims Robert Kroutil, a longtime ASPECT scientist who helped develop the program and later became a whistleblower. “It’s such an key program, and they've allowed it to waste away to nothing.”.

The EPA did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview or questions about ASPECT’s decline, its handling of emergencies, the replacement of its sensors, and allegations of mismanagement by former program scientists and managers.

The country’s need for a chemical-sensing plane grew from the smoldering, toxic debris in Manhattan on September 11, 2001, when the EPA’s monitoring trucks were stranded on the wrong side of the Hudson River, unable to cross after bridges and tunnels into the city closed.

Kroutil was a program manager for the Department of Defense at the time, leading a research team that had developed the technology that would become ASPECT, short for Airborne Spectral Photometric Environmental Collection Technology.

The military transferred the program to the EPA for use in detecting hazardous chemicals during civilian emergencies.

It became a critical tool for emergency responders over the next 20 years.

For 72 hours after Hurricane Katrina struck, it was the only emergency response aircraft flying over New Orleans, where it helped locate a missing 55-gallon drum of potentially lethal chloroacetic acid.

During the Deepwater Horizon disaster, it became a key tool for tracking oil slicks in the Gulf of Mexico.

And when a fire engulfed 15 massive tanks at a chemical storage terminal east of Houston in 2019, the ASPECT plane helped emergency responders track the plume, which contained the carcinogen benzene.

Richard Lawhorn, an assistant chief with Harris County’s hazardous materials response team in Texas, indicates the plane could detect chemicals at elevations beyond the reach of ground crews and survey a much wider area in a short time. Unlike ground monitors, the plane can scan a swath of air three-quarters of a mile wide, capturing a far broader picture of potential hazards.

“They’re monitoring the products we can’t reach,” he states.

Industry observers note that the program’s success lay in its intellectual rigor: Kroutil and the program’s radiological lead held PhDs, as did Mark Thomas, the former EPA official. The team wrote the code, designed the mounts that held gear, and analyzed the raw data themselves.

“We were very, very hands-on and intimately familiar with every part of that aircraft,” notes Thomas, who later went to work for a tech giant that develops chemical-sensing technology.

The decline began with the departures of key ASPECT personnel during President Donald Trump’s first administration.

As part of an agency reorganization, the EPA told the program’s staff in 2019 that they had to relocate to Texas, where the plane was based, or face termination, documents show.

The mandate was unnecessary, according to Thomas, because the program had been designed for remote operation. Rather than leave his elderly parents in Kansas, he retired. Then, ASPECT’s radiological lead left the division, and the engineer who helped build and manage the plane’s sensors accepted a demotion to stay in Kansas.

According to Kroutil and two of his former colleagues, the EPA then failed to fill those vacancies with scientists who had any experience with airborne chemical detection.

“They lost the institutional knowledge of the program, and quite frankly, lost the momentum of the program,” Thomas indicates.

Industry observers note that during its first two decades, the plane flew almost 80 emergency missions—an average of roughly four a year. In the past five years, however, it has flown an average of just one a year.

In October, hundreds were evacuated—and more than 50 were treated at hospitals—when a 5,500-gallon industrial tank in Toledo, Ohio, leaked glycidyl methacrylate, a chemical used in making plastics that is a probable carcinogen suspected of causing genetic defects. It was one of at least 80 chemical emergencies this year that the plane did not respond to.

Recent findings suggest that the decline comes as accidental chemical releases are becoming more common. The US Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 last year, up from 83 in 2021.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, has proposed rolling back federal safeguards designed to prevent chemical disasters, including requirements for some plants to undergo independent safety audits and provide hazard information to nearby communities.

According to recent reports, former ASPECT program managers say they used to actively track chemical emergencies and urge EPA on-scene coordinators—who manage environmental emergencies—to deploy the plane. After they left, that proactive approach vanished: The plane stayed in a Texas hangar until coordinators requested it, they say.

Scott Smith, an independent environmental tester who’s often called on by local communities to investigate chemical contamination after industrial accidents, indicates ASPECT could help him target his soil and water testing by mapping the path of chemical plumes. Deployed regularly, he says, the plane could save lives. Instead, “it's being shut down and not used.”.

On February 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train carrying the carcinogen vinyl chloride and other hazardous chemicals derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, near the Pennsylvania border.

As fires from the derailment smoldered, emergency responders feared an explosion—and made the controversial decision to vent and burn five railcars containing vinyl chloride, sending a towering plume over the town.

Sources indicate that ASPECT missed the vent-and-burn operation, and its services weren’t requested until more than two days after the initial disaster. Even then, it was used sparingly. Despite the derailment being one of the nation’s worst chemical disasters in years, Kroutil indicates, the plane collected just eight minutes of chemical data when it finally flew over East Palestine on February 7—a fraction of what it typically gathered during an emergency.

Had the plane been deployed earlier—or flown over the site en route to Pittsburgh, the nearest major airport—its thermal detection equipment might have helped determine that the tank cars were not in danger of exploding, Kroutil later stated in an affidavit.

Sources indicate that the National Transportation Safety Board concluded that the vent-and-burn operation had been unnecessary. It found no evidence of the dangerous chemical reaction that Norfolk Southern and its contractors stated threatened an explosion. Temperature readings indicated the railcars were cooling.

An EPA inspector general investigation later found a series of errors in the East Palestine response: The agency had poorly documented its procedures and failed to adequately inform emergency responders of the plane’s capabilities. The on-scene coordinator, who didn’t request the plane until two days after the derailment, wrongly believed that ground-level monitoring would provide better data.

Frustrated by how EPA officials were running the program, Kroutil retired. Two of his colleagues also left, further draining the program’s pool of experience and expertise.

On August 22, 2025, a massive explosion ripped through Smitty’s Supply, a facility that blended and packaged oil and other engine lubricants in Roseland, Louisiana.

According to recent reports, less than 4 miles away, Ronnie Polezcek and his family heard something hitting their roof that afternoon. At first, they thought it was raindrops.

But when they walked outside, Polezcek says, “It was just like it was raining oil.”.

The dark residue covered the family’s 23-acre farm. Polezcek notes he had to burn his hay, move his cows temporarily to Mississippi, and replace a metal roof that could not be scrubbed clean. Two of his cows miscarried soon afterward, he says, and a veterinarian found arsenic in one of them. Polezcek filed a lawsuit against Smitty’s in September 2025 that has been consolidated into an ongoing class-action case.

The Smitty’s fire burned for nearly two weeks, sending a huge plume of smoke into the air. Local authorities ordered a 1-mile evacuation around the plant, and the EPA dispatched ASPECT—the plane’s first emergency deployment in 19 months.

In a recent development, the agency didn’t publicly post findings from the ASPECT flights until August 31, nine days after the fire began. Those reports show the air around Smitty’s contained ozone and three other pollutants but at levels far below those considered harmful to human health.

A later analysis of the raw flight data, though, told a very different story.

Working with the Government Accountability Project, a nonprofit that advocates for whistleblowers, Kroutil obtained data from ASPECT’s third flight over the disaster area. He states it took him weeks to analyze it, doing by hand what the plane’s software was designed to do in minutes.

According to recent reports, kroutil identified high concentrations of the neurotoxicant toluene and the carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene, among other toxic chemicals. He concluded that the levels of toluene were so high, they could have put nearby communities at risk.

Many of the findings also matched what Smith, the independent environmental tester, detected in soil and water after the fire.

The EPA later acknowledged a similar problem, according to records that the Government Accountability Project obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

In a May 2026 email, an EPA manager noted some target chemicals might have been present in data from the third flight but weren't flagged at the time the data was collected. The manager suggested that deterioration of the aging sensors might have contributed to the failure.

Polezcek believes officials should have evacuated a larger area.

According to recent reports, “I really think it was a pitiful job,” he says. “They just kept saying, ‘There’s nothing to worry about, you’re good to go.’”.

In June, the EPA inspector general confirmed that Kroutil’s warnings were justified: The plane could no longer provide chemical-monitoring data within five minutes.

It has been revealed that instead, scientists had to conduct manual analysis that would take about a week. The EPA also failed to tell on-scene coordinators that the program isn’t working as designed.

EPA officials blamed the delays on old sensors. The agency bypassed competitive bidding to award a Canadian manufacturer, Telops, a $1.7 million contract for replacement sensors designed for several applications, including gas detection and mineral mapping. Integrating the newly introduced sensors won’t be complete until “early to mid 2027,” according to the EPA.

Recent findings suggest that in contract documents, the EPA cited peer-reviewed studies showing the Telops sensors had been field-tested and proven. But much of the research on the fresh equipment has focused on tracking methane leaks, not the wide range of toxic chemicals released during complex industrial emergencies.

Five people formerly involved with ASPECT have raised concerns that the upcoming sensors will be less capable than the old ones at detecting hazardous chemicals during industrial emergencies.

Exosens, the parent firm of Telops, told Floodlight that its system and the old one use “different measurement architectures.”.

The latest sensors, it says, can identify hundreds of chemicals and distinguish chemical plumes from surrounding objects. The original infrared sensors, built by the Canadian firm Bomem, were rebuilt multiple times and equipped with new software.

Chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert with no ties to Telops, the EPA, or the firm where Thomas now works, indicates the new Telops sensors could complement ASPECT’s older sensors but would be a poor replacement. They are slower, less sensitive, and less suited to moving targets, he says.

“To say, ‘We're just going to replace these other two instruments’ … I mean, that’s ludicrous,” he claims.

It has been revealed that the old sensors had problems, too. Their artificial intelligence software had not been retrained after an electrical malfunction several years ago, Kroutil and Thomas say. In early 2023, contract scientists with the program presented the EPA with a strategy to retrain the software, emails show. But the EPA never took the required steps, according to Kroutil and Rick Turville, a former ASPECT manager who left the program in 2025.

According to recent reports, kroutil and his former colleagues say they have no confidence that the new sensors will fix the problem. They expect the program to deteriorate further.

In the affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project, Kroutil offers a dim prognosis: “Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the ASPECT program, it is not going to get any better and EPA will be flying blind.”.

Uber may be breaking up with Waymo, but it’s also gaining a latest robotaxi BFF: Amazon. Starting today, Uber riders in Las Vegas can be matched with Amazon-owned Zoox’s purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxis.

It’s a first for both companies: the first time Uber is adding a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle to its network, and the first time that Zoox is opening up its fleet to a third-party app. Uber says that anyone ordering an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save in Sin City can get matched with a Zoox at no extra charge. Just like with Uber’s other AV partnerships (like Waymo in Phoenix and Austin, for now), riders can toggle a preference in the app’s Ride Preferences settings to boost their chances of getting an autonomous pod.

Sources indicate that unlike Uber’s human drivers, Zoox has some geographic limitations. The company’s robotaxis only cover heavy tourist zones, like the Strip, downtown Las Vegas, and the Arts District. And Zoox isn’t abandoning its standalone app; it will continue to operate independently alongside the Uber integration.

Alongside the launch, Uber and Zoox announced a multiyear deal making them the official rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts International in Las Vegas. Anyone who has ever tried to catch a ride at the Bellagio or MGM Grand knows that resort pickup zones are notoriously chaotic. For autonomous vehicles, navigating sprawling, poorly mapped casino entrances — where valets, idling tour buses, and confused tourists all mill about — is a major technical headache.

Industry observers note that to keep Zoox’s pods from getting stuck in endless resort traffic loops, the partnership goes beyond simple branding. MGM, Uber, and Zoox say they are rolling out physical infrastructure tweaks, like clearer on-property wayfinding and custom in-app guidance designed to make pickups and drop-offs actually work smoothly for driverless cars.

Uber and Zoox aren’t stopping at Vegas. The two companies already have their eyes their next major market: Los Angeles. Zoox aims to launch initial standalone operations in LA through its own app before the end of 2026, followed by a full Uber integration sometime in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that uber’s playbook of welcoming a variety of small and large robotaxi players into its app came after the company pivoted away from building its own self-driving tech. Now it’s attempting to position itself as an indispensable platform for every autonomous vehicle operator, including Motional, WeRide, Avride, and Zoox.

In a recent development, of course, Uber’s strategy has had some drawbacks, too. Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana recently confirmed an end to her organization’s exclusive partnership with Uber in Austin and Atlanta by January 2028, calling it a “crapshoot.”.

#369. The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya

The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers.
  • On the island of Fresh Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round.
  • According to recent reports, positioned in the tropics beside the largest expanse of warm ocean water on Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers.

On the island of Fresh Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers.

According to recent reports, positioned in the tropics beside the largest expanse of warm ocean water on Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round. Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “canaries in the coal mine,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, and the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.

The change on Puncak Jaya is visible in this image pair, acquired in 1988 by the TM (Thematic Mapper) on Landsat 5 (left) and in 2026 by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 (right). The false-color images help distinguish areas of ice (light blue) from exposed bedrock (brown). Clouds appear white and vegetation green.

In 1988, the glaciers covered about 4.31 square kilometers (1.66 square miles), according to Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). By September 2025, satellite and aerial data showed that only about 0.09 square kilometers (0.03 square miles) remained—an area equivalent to about a dozen soccer fields. That’s roughly 2 percent of the 1988 extent. An aerial survey planned for December should yield an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, Permana stated.

Industry observers note that the glaciers have thinned, too. Measurements at the primary monitoring site on the East Northwall Firn indicated a drop from 32 meters (105 feet) thick in 2010 to 4 meters (13 feet) in 2023, Permana stated. By November 2024, the ice at this site was gone.

According to recent reports, as the glaciers thin, they also break apart, and each upcoming fragment adds exposed edges where ice can melt, compounding the losses. In the 2026 Landsat image, freshly uncovered bedrock appears between the remnants. Snow still falls in the area, but it doesn’t last long enough on the bare rock to build up into new ice.

“It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has tracked Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite imagery. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”.

To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts. Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.

“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said.

Industry observers note that as for the remaining patches of ice, time will tell how long they last. Recent satellite studies suggest complete disappearance of the main glacial ice areas could occur around 2030. Permana noted that BMKG estimates suggest they could be gone much sooner, hastened by the current El Niño.

According to recent reports, past El Niño years have hit these glaciers especially hard. As the air warms, the freezing level rises above the summit, so precipitation falls as rain instead of snow. That means less fresh white snow that normally reflects sunlight and shields the ice, leaving darker surfaces that absorb more heat and melt faster. During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than usual, losing roughly 5.3 meters (17 feet) of thickness in a single year. The 2023-2024 El Niño brought another bout of rapid thinning, about 2 to 4 meters (7 to 13 feet) per year.

Sources indicate that NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Kathryn Hansen.

Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.﻿.

According to recent reports, for years, Jensen Huang has had an almost unprecedented power to shape AI’s advancement as Nvidia’s CEO, cofounder, and president. As The Verge wrote last week, Nvidia’s chips are “the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built.” Ever-increasing demand has consistently outpaced supply, leading AI CEOs to essentially bow at Huang’s feet as they vie for more compute ahead of their much-hyped IPOs. Nvidia also has a varied investment portfolio of up-and-coming AI companies from neoclouds to infrastructure firms, worth nearly $100 billion, and Huang has President Donald Trump’s ear. He’s even been called Trump’s “most influential adviser” when it comes to technology. As of last Wednesday, however, Huang — a pivotal figure in the industry — is no longer CEO of Nvidia.

Since Huang’s resignation last week, the scandal over his multiple affairs has shown no sign of waning. After the announcement, Nvidia shares dropped 14 percent, making it one of the worst weeks on the market for the tech giant in the past year and a half. And the revelations kept coming. Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported that Huang had had a third affair with a second employee (though the employee was unnamed). We learned that Huang had reportedly misled Nvidia leaders about his infidelity, that Nvidia was allegedly linked to the supply of nearly $12 billion of its chips to China, and that alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang’s companies reportedly promised advanced chips to Chinese AI company DeepSeek.

In a recent development, there’s reportedly been a petition to bring back Huang by some Nvidia employees, as well as reports of Huang assembling a “war room” of allies to float a comeback as Nvidia CEO. Lawmakers have begun investigations into the alleged chip-smuggling and other offenses. Every day, there’s increasing evidence of fallout inside the Trump administration. And as Nvidia’s quarterly earnings on Tuesday loom, the future of the company and the AI industry as a whole remain in flux.

What does an Nvidia without Huang look like? It’s hard to say, since he’s been at the helm for 33 years. CFO Colette Kress has taken on the role of interim CEO, and the broader AI world is waiting to see where one of the world’s most valuable companies — and one that helped shape the industry’s every milestone — goes from here.

Sources indicate that nvidia is such a large tech giant that the implications of Huang’s departure “will take years to play out,” noted Stephen Straus, CEO of KUNGFU.AI, an AI consulting firm. “[Nvidia has] their market share … they have the world’s best chips, they have the most manufacturing capacity … and they have a whole ecosystem built around what they’ve done. None of that changes with one person.” While there’s been discussion of Huang’s departure speeding along an AI bubble burst, Straus compares the situation to the dot-com bust — which didn’t stop the growth of the internet itself.

Recent findings suggest that huang’s resignation may not cause a domino effect in AI, but longer-term AI funding initiatives championed by him may eventually be affected, states Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm. Huang championed fundraising for the broader AI buildout: In August, Nvidia signed deals with six large financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund AI infrastructure expansion, and those agreements or future ones could look different if “the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals,” wrote Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello in a note last week on Monday.

Some lawmakers were already planning to pull CEOs before Congress.

It has been revealed that far downstream of the biggest companies, smaller AI startups are wondering how the effects will trickle down. Michal Miernowski, co-founder and CEO of Amperos Health, which builds AI agents for healthcare billing, sits in the applied AI space about two layers removed from Nvidia. Recent findings suggest that some new lawmakers already planned to haul CEOs to Capitol Hill to testify under oath. The revelations around Huang, a major Trump ally, provide an early opportunity to take action.

“We want to see a Democratic Congress investigate Nvidia for anti-competitive practices that pass off costs to consumers, what the organization knew about chip smuggling operations with China, and what Nvidia received in exchange for donations to the Trump campaign and ballroom,” Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project, told The Verge.

Recent findings suggest that AI safety researchers also worry that in the worst-case scenario, the instability around last week’s events could speed up potentially dangerous AI milestones like recursive self-improvement, i.e., powerful AI that can autonomously improve and build future versions of itself. Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, an AI safety firm and third-party auditor, said he worries that the volatility stemming from Huang’s departure “actually increases loss of control risk because companies feel even more revenue pressure and therefore are more willing to cut corners on safety.”.

In a recent development, early last week, before Huang’s resignation, the general consensus among Silicon Valley heavyweights, analysts, and politicians was that Huang’s “irreplaceable” impact would mean a return to the status quo for Nvidia. Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote in a note that day that the firm “can’t rule out … Nvidia returning to business as usual” since Huang is the “only CEO the firm has ever known.” Now, as Huang reportedly assembles allies to push for a comeback the likes of which haven’t been seen since the 2023 Sam Altman coup, the entire AI industry is waiting to see which way it will go.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As creative software races toward increased automation, are we as designers asking the right questions?

Over the years, I’ve watched the conversations of web developers and designers shift increasingly toward technology, and further away from something we once took great pride in: Craft.

Recent findings suggest that the 20th century was an extraordinary period for graphic design, particularly typography and print. By the 1990s we had inherited an astonishingly mature digital toolbox: QuarkXPress, Photoshop, PostScript typography and all the precision that came with them.

Those tools were deeply rooted in the crafts they replaced. Photoshop borrowed directly from the photographic darkroom – dodge, burn and all. Quark brought centuries of typographic practice into the digital workspace, giving designers extraordinarily precise control over type and composition.

Then we moved communications to the web – and somehow left much of that toolbox behind. Our web platforms never came close to giving designers the same depth of control. Many creatives simply accepted the loss and said, “Well, that’s just the web.”.

I never quite bought into that. Instead I started making notes for what would become Design Studio for Gutenberg (DSG), a powerful designer-first plugin for WordPress Gutenberg.

And at this moment, an inflection point when creative software makers increasingly want to automate design itself, we need to ask: Could better tools offer another way forward?

Web typography has always been a particular sore point for me.

In a recent development, I’ll admit my standards may be unusually high. I cut my typography chops as a Type Director at J. Walter Type, part of the legendary JWT ad agency, and such training is hard to shake.

It has been revealed that so I found workarounds for maintaining the quality my clients expected. For example, for important headlines I would often set the type in Illustrator, kern it properly, export it as SVG artwork and bring that into a website as art.

In a recent development, ridiculous? Perhaps. But my clients included brands like American Express, Merck and Lincoln Center. They expected high-quality work, and I delivered. But there had to be a better way.

As each fresh web-design platform arrived, I would look to see whether somebody had finally built one from a designer’s point of view. A typographer's point of view. Many claimed they had. But mostly they just gave us what programmers thought designers wanted.

Recent findings suggest that eventually I stopped waiting. A few years ago I sat down with my studio’s programmers and gave them a simple directive:We are going to build what designers need.

WordPress was the obvious foundation. It was open source, mature and unlikely to disappear like so many web-dev programs before it.

Recent findings suggest that my other directive: Design Studio could not be another heavy page-builder sitting on top of WordPress. It needed to live inside Gutenberg and thus benefit from WordPress’ lighter weight and faster core.

It has been revealed that we even created our own mantra: WordPress Builds Webpages. DSG Designs Them.

We methodically broke down what was missing. The list grew fast.

We ultimately ended up creating a system with THREE BLOCKS, one custom TEMPLATE, and more UI additions and tools than I could count.

Let’s start with the three blocks, which contain tools you simply will not find in other web-development systems:.

In a recent development, this text block is unique. It has every major type control that you might have found in Quark or InDesign. Powerful tools like KERNING, without which we can never hope to produce professional grade typography.

Font choices in TDB are not tied to any template. Instead they allow full font and style selections just like a desktop app. And it works directly with our font management system found in the DESIGNER DASH backend (more on that later).

It also allows mixed type, font, style and more, all within a single text container.

A friend testing DSG at a major ad agency stated it best: “Composite layers in WP? Mind blown.”.

Import multilayer Photoshop or Krita files (see my comparison of those two here), then treat each layer independently with blur, invert, halftone, sepia and full BLEND settings. Then each layer can be easily scaled, rotated, and even placed anywhere on the page.

This tool is simply fun. Go play with it in our LIVE DEMO.

It has been revealed that this full-width block offers real freedom. Starting with a HEIGHT CONTROL slider, so no more needing to wedge in spacers or scaffolding.

Within the Composition Block, TDB and ADB can be placed freely anywhere you want. Even overlapping each other, or hanging off the CB. (Our website is the perfect example.).

Some early testers had to look twice to make sure they were still in WordPress.

Recent findings suggest that we knew just what they meant: Rulers, Guides, Grid, device-specific Visibility icons across every object in the List View. We include a very special BLANK CANVAS template, better page controls, and a backend DESIGNER DASH with tabs for Font.

Industry observers note that my goal here isn’t to catalog every Design Studio for Gutenberg feature. I mention these to make a larger point: Web designers deserve better tools. And that feels particularly important now.

AI has an enormous role to play in our future creative work. Let it remove drudgery, generate first passes, organise assets and automate anything that doesn’t benefit from human judgment.

But craft begins where the default answer ends. “Craft” has always been, and shall always remain a very human thing.

Craft is deciding that two letters need to be kerned tighter. That an image needs to move three pixels down. That this composition should deliberately break the grid. That the mobile version shouldn’t simply be a smaller copy of the desktop.

Those are precisely the kinds of decisions that only professional designers should make. And it requires precision tools like those in DSG that allow such decisions to be executed.

After reading the DSG manual, I asked ChatGPT how its own web-building abilities compared with those of a competent designer using DSG. Its answer was spot-on:.

“A surprising amount of what DSG enables is still awkward to get from AI.” — ChatGPT.

In my mind it is not a question of human vs. AI. But instead, how to use the best tools for each part of your job.

We built a live demo so you can come kick the tires. And because we are very massive on sharing in general, and the open source, free and affordable software movements, we are releasing Design Studio for Gutenberg, with everything we have talked about and so much more for just $39. Including per-person unlimited use (right, that means no more counting websites), and a license that never expires.

Recent findings suggest that with the release of Design Studio 1.0 we hope to contribute to the goal of building a better web. This is step one.

Visit Design Studio for Gutenberg, try the DEMO: https://openstudiony.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut.

Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

"Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado tech giant that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9).

Industry observers note that the FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated. (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet rapidly rising demand for debuts and landings.).

For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated.

The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service.

The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future.

Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur, the successor to the venerable Atlas V.

Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit.

The manufacturer is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that strategy to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef.

Industry observers note that elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an important difference between human and chimpanzee brain development.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population.
  • It has been revealed that although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an important difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene that remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in the developing brain.

The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population. They also offer fresh clues about how the brains of humans and our closest evolutionary relatives may have developed differently.

It has been revealed that although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years. Some of these ancient infections left traces of viral DNA that continue to influence how genes function today.

Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University, notes the discovery demonstrates how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population.

"The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is notable to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development," notes Johan Jakobsson.

How an Ancient Virus Silenced a Brain Development Gene.

At the center of the discovery is a gene called LINC00662. Researchers found that it is active during early human brain development but completely switched off in comparable chimpanzee brain models.

The difference appears to be caused by a genetic remnant of PTERV1, an ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago. PTERV1 belongs to a group known as endogenous retroviruses, which are viruses whose genetic material became incorporated into the DNA of their hosts. Once embedded in the genome, these viral sequences can be inherited by future generations.

Sources indicate that over time, PTERV1 produced numerous copies of its genetic material that became scattered across different parts of the chimpanzee genome. Researchers found that these viral sequences are systematically silenced through a process called methylation.

Recent findings suggest that methylation involves chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity. It is one of the ways cells control which genetic instructions are used and which remain inactive. In this case, the ancient viral insertion appears to have caused a neighboring gene involved in brain development to be switched off.

Jakobsson says understanding these differences in gene regulation could also provide important insights into how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.

Miniature Brains Reveal a Striking Genetic Difference.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the virus's effects, researchers grew miniature brain models called organoids using stem cells from humans and chimpanzees. These three-dimensional structures reproduce certain features of developing brain tissue, allowing scientists to study aspects of early brain development under controlled laboratory conditions.

When the team compared the two types of organoids, the difference was striking. LINC00662 showed strong activity in the human brain models but was completely inactive in those derived from chimpanzee cells.

"The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids," says Patricia Gerdes, postdoc in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The researchers then set out to determine whether the ancient viral DNA was directly responsible for this difference.

Using CRISPR-Cas9, a powerful gene editing technology that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the viral sequence from chimpanzee cells.

In a recent development, the result provided compelling evidence. Once the viral DNA was removed, the previously inactive LINC00662 gene switched back on.

"This indicates that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees," says Patricia Gerdes.

Latest Clues to Human Brain Evolution.

The team also wanted to understand what LINC00662 actually does in the human brain. To investigate, they used CRISPR to switch off the gene in human brain organoids and examined how other genes responded.

Recent findings suggest that disabling LINC00662 reduced the activity of genes associated with nerve cell development and the formation of connections between neurons. These processes are essential for establishing the networks that allow the brain to communicate and function.

The results suggest that LINC00662 contributes to important stages of early human brain development, while the ancient viral insertion prevents the gene from functioning in chimpanzees.

More broadly, the discovery highlights an important principle of evolution. Although humans and chimpanzees share much of their genetic material, differences in how genes are switched on and off can influence how their bodies and brains develop.

The findings suggest that ancient viral infections may have contributed to these differences by altering gene regulation long after the original infections disappeared.

Researchers now strategy to investigate whether other remnants of ancient viruses have similarly influenced brain evolution. They also hope to determine whether these inherited viral sequences may play a role in neurological diseases.

Together, the discoveries raise an intriguing possibility that some of the differences between human and chimpanzee brains may trace back, at least in part, to viruses that infected our evolutionary relatives millions of years ago.

Explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light. Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds -- and some then explode. Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image, with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right -- in the red region. Jets and winds likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most notable and when.Tomorrow's picture: sky duel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Digital photo frames aren't new technology, but they're still one of my favorite pieces of tech to put into a home. These devices promise something simple: a beautiful frame to display all the photos sitting on your camera roll, displayed for you to enjoy at any time.

Best of all, you don't have to settle for just a digital photo frame anymore. While my favorite digital photo frames from Aura excel at displaying your photos (and keeping your life subscription-free!), there's a nice variety of options if you want something that displays your pictures and does a little more, too. Want something that doubles as a family calendar or has a voice assistant to answer your questions? This guide has picks for that. Want something totally wireless? I've tested those, too.

Here are all the best photo frames I've tried over years of testing. Looking for more home gadgets? Don't miss our guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars, Best Smart Speakers, and Best Sunrise Alarm Clocks.

In a recent development, love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

I've been testing digital photo frames for almost six years now and always sing their praises. These devices are designed to look like a regular photo frame, but with a screen inside that displays whichever photos you send to it. There's always an app involved to upload images, and you can also usually send photos over email, too. Both the email option and the app let you invite other family members to the frame, so multiple people can send images. It's perfect for families living in the same house or for long-distance family members who want to share their best pictures with Grandma.

I also like that these devices are fairly intuitive and minimal. Digital photo frames simply connect to your Wi-Fi and display your photos. There are also options that can do multiple things if you want a multipurpose device in your home, but your frame doesn't have to do anything but show your photos.

Sources indicate that do you have any photos on a digital device, like a smartphone, computer, or camera? Or does someone in your family have photos they could send to you or directly to the frame itself? Then yes, a digital photo frame is absolutely worth buying. If you have photos you take and want to see regularly or wish you had all your wedding photos on display instead of just the ones that fit on your wall, a digital photo frame will easily solve that for you.

In a recent development, they're also great to purchase as a gift. I've given two different digital photo frames to my parents over the years and am presently helping my mother pick one out to gift my grandmother to enjoy photos in her nursing home. It's a great gift for young parents, too, who have camera rolls packed with photos of their fresh baby (or their fur baby!) and photo aficionados who will never have enough frames in their house for their work.

There's no beating Aura when it comes to digital frames, and it's the option I recommend most to everyone in my life after using Aura's frames since 2021. All of them have high-quality displays and unlimited photo storage, a combo you won't find anywhere else. Aura's frames are simple to set up, use, and share with family and friends, too. Everything is controlled with the app, so there's no laggy touchscreen to futz with—you can scroll through or heart photos using the touch bar on top and use the app to control how quickly your photos change and other settings. My frames are shared with my husband, but I can also scroll down and see my parents’ frames that they've shared with me, all in one application.

It has been revealed that aura has had a lot of frame designs over the years, but it’s focused now on its mat-style frames that look fantastic in your home. These frames all have different names, but are nearly identical otherwise. The 10-inch Carver Mat ($179) is a mat version of the popular affordable Carver frame, and it sits in a landscape mode that will show vertical photos side by side. The other two are the 12-inch Aspen ($229) and 15-inch Walden ($299), which are flat on the back so that they can be mounted on a wall in either landscape or portrait mode. I've tried all three, and my personal favorite is the Walden for my home, but that's since I have one massive great room that encompasses the dining room, kitchen, and living room, and the Walden sits in a far corner but is easily visible from any point in the room. If you're working with a more normal room size, the Carver and Aspen are both great sizes, but I do like that the Aspen can be rotated to portrait or landscape orientation; the Carver will only do landscape, and can't be wall-mounted, either. It's up to you if that's worth spending more.

Recent findings suggest that no matter which model you choose, the best part about the Aura frames is that they don't look like shiny computer screens nor are they haunted by the blue tinge you'll find on cheaper digital frames. Especially thanks to the mat style you'll find on these three models, they can easily pass for a real photo—until the picture changes, of course. There's really no better experience you can find in the world of digital photo frames.

I've liked Skylight's photo frames well enough, but my favorite product from Skylight is its digital wall calendars. These calendars double as digital photo frames and digital wall calendars since you can set up a photo screensaver to pop up when you aren't interacting with it. The only downside is you'll have to pay a subscription fee to use the photo feature, but all of Skylight's devices have some kind of paywall associated with them.

Recent findings suggest that the Skylight Calendar 2 is the newest of its three calendar models, but feels like the Goldilocks option with its 15-inch screen that's a good size for kitchen countertops or to mount on the wall, faster performance compared to older models, a more reasonable price point (the Skylight Calendar Max has a wild price tag), and interchangeable snap frames so you can adjust the look of your device to match your current home aesthetic. It's a great device that has made it easy to peek at my family's calendar whenever I want, and my son uses the Skylight Buddy in his room to track his own daily routine, but I could also teach him to just use the Calendar 2 for it instead. While the screen isn't as matte as the Aura frames, photos still look great on this screen, and the uploader tool is easy to use.

According to recent reports, if you like the idea of Skylight but don't want a subscription to have the photo feature (and don't mind missing out on the calendar and chores), you can get the Skylight Frame 2 ($190). There's still a subscription option for that model for certain features, like making albums and having a cloud backup, but you don't need it to have the basic digital photo frame experience. The Frame-only subscription is cheaper than the calendar one—$39 a year for Frame Plus versus $79 a year for Calendar Plus—but you get less, since the Calendar Plus subscription includes meal planning, an AI uploading tool, and more. I like Skylight's options a lot, especially with the new calendar-based ecosystem, but the subscription fee is the main downside. But you can get a lot more features out of your device.

I didn't expect to like Amazon's newly introduced Alexa Photo Frame. I thought it would be gimmicky and frustrating to use, especially as someone who's hated Amazon's photo uploader tool in the past for its smart displays. But I found myself surprisingly pleased not only with the frame itself, but even the smart speaker experience built into it. It does help that I already have an Amazon Prime subscription, which you'll want to have unlimited photo storage and to get Alexa+ voice access on the device.

Sources indicate that what helps is that the Alexa Photo Frame uses the Amazon Photos app. It's similar to the Google Photos app in that it wants to back up all your photos for you from your phone, and it also connects to and controls this newly introduced digital photo frame. (I can also control which photos are added to my other Alexa smart displays through the app under the devices tab, so it's not exclusive to the Alexa Photo Frame.) I uploaded a handful of photos to the frame and was impressed with how nice the experience looked. The display looked a little more matte than my Skylight Calendar 2 when I put them side by side, and it has a mat-style frame that reminds me of the Aura frames. The Alexa Photo Frame has only a 10.1-inch screen, and no option to rotate it between landscape or portrait; the included stand puts it into landscape mode only, making it much like the Aura Carver Mat in specs and design. It does not, however, have a Photo Match option, so the paired vertical photos can look a bit random.

The Alexa Photo Frame also costs more than the Carver, since it comes with an extra bonus: Amazon's AI-powered voice assistant, Alexa+. I was impressed that even though this device is flat enough to be wall-mounted, Alexa's voice still sounded full and clear without any tinny quality, and music actually sounded pretty good too. I'd prefer a real speaker, but if you wanted one device for just photos and simple questions without any other screen clutter, this is a good option. This device is best for Prime owners who will get Alexa+ for free and free photo storage to boot.

Aura came out with the first Aura Ink frame last fall, and I was impressed by its unique color E Ink screen and fully wireless experience that made it a frame I was actually willing to mount on my wall. As of this week, Aura has a new addition to its cordless Ink lineup: the Ink 10-inch, which has a smaller screen, expanded color palette, and 200 pixels-per-inch resolution.

Like the Aura frames I recommend throughout this story, the Aura Ink 10-inch has unlimited storage and is run through Aura's clean, intuitive app that has no subscription tiers. But the Ink 10-inch (and the larger Ink 13-inch) use an E Ink screen like a color e-reader does to run on a battery, so you can place the frame anywhere without needing to constantly plug it in. While the Ink 10-inch is smaller, it has a latest nine-color e-paper display that adds off-white, mustard yellow, and orange to its color wheel. It still has a newspaper-like look to it, and Aura's technology will run photos through its algorithm to convert them onto the e-paper screen.

The Aura Ink defaults to only show one photo a day to preserve battery life and because the transition to change photos takes longer than on a standard screen. But the Ink 10-inch does have a prettier, melt-like transition effect instead of the flashing that the Ink 13-inch does when it switches photos overnight. There's also a subtle front light in both the Ink 10-inch and Ink 13-inch, but it looks best when hit with natural light to help illuminate it. It's a great option if you want something that won't have a cord and don't mind a newspaper-like look. It looks more realistic than other frames with this e-paper screen; friends of mine have genuinely been shocked when I tell them it's a digital frame.

The Aura Carver has been around for a while, and it's still a great frame. The 10-inch frame is one of the best cheap frames you can find, pairing Aura's fantastic experience (a great app! unlimited storage!) with a smaller, landscape-only option. While it does have a slimmer aspect ratio of 16:10, landscape photos still look good, and you can toggle on Photo Match in the settings to have the frame “match” to similar portrait orientation photos together to fill the screen. It'll often match by event or match two photos of the same person together.

The Aura Carver also has the Carver Mat ($179) version for a little higher price tag that matches the aesthetic of the other mat versions and is included as part of our top pick. But if you're looking for the cheapest option while still getting the great experience Aura offers, the base Aura Carver is the cheapest you'll find. It's also often on sale during events like Black Friday, so keep an eye out.

It has been revealed that nixplay Classic 10.1-Inch Frame for $190: Nixplay is semi-comparable to Aura, with a range of digital photo frames that's been around for years. But you will be hit with a subscription fee if you want more than 500 MB of photos on your device—Nixplay Lite costs $20 a year for 100 GB, while Nixplay Plus costs $30 for unlimited photo storage. You'll get other features, too, like ability to add longer video clips and connect to more frames, but the storage aspect is the part you'll run into after using this frame for a long time. I tested the Classic 10.1" Frame that's been around for a while, and while it's easy and intuitive to use, I found the settings slow to enhancement from changes I make in the app, and I don't like the distracting transitions the frame will use by default. It also has a surprising amount of border for vertical photos in portrait mode. It's still a fine frame overall, especially if you're able to manage your storage usage, but it remains only an honorable mention for me still. Plus, you can get the Aura Carver for cheaper for the same size screen and unlimited storage (but you won't get a touchscreen or ability to rotate between portrait and landscape modes, which the Nixplay Classic can do).

In a recent development, skylight Frame 2 for $190: Skylight's photo frames are where the company originated, but I do prefer its calendars over its photo frames. The Frame 2 is its latest generation, and the best part is that you can swap out the frames, which Skylight named Snap Frames (starting at $15), to match the style of your home. You can upload photos by app or email, but you will need a subscription—Frame Plus, which costs $39 a year—to create albums, adjust settings using the app, upload videos, and add captions. The subscription doesn't control your actual storage, and instead the Frame 2 has a limit of 16 GB of storage.

Aura Mason for $199: The massive original favorite from Aura, with a solid frame and the ability to rotate between landscape and portrait mode. It's still a great frame, but Aura did say they're sunsetting the model, but it'll remain available until it's sold out. It's still available so far.

Sources indicate that azorpa 10-Inch Digital Photo Frame for $90: This slim frame works well and has a nice affordable price point, and it can be rotated. It also has its own dedicated app, unlike several affordable models that all use the same Frameo app. But the ratio is slimmer than smartphone photos, so I found myself needing to constantly recrop pictures or have an extra border along two of the sides. If you don't mind a border and want a really cheap frame, this one's solid.

Cozyla frames: Our staffers have tried a few digital photo frames from this brand, and one of its digital wall calendars. Photo quality was great and there were solid features like only showing photos that match the current orientation of the frame. Our reviewer found the app to be frustrating, however, and it comes preloaded with unnecessary art images.

In a recent development, familink 10-Inch Digital Photo Frame for $200: Familink's frame works with or without an internet connection, thanks to its 4G SIM card. Someone will need to set up an account on the website or app (iOS, Android) so that family members can send photos (or even chats) to the frame. There was no slideshow feature when we tested it in 2024, but the screen still looked good.

According to recent reports, loop Family Frame for $200: This is a good option if you want to text photos to a display, instead of using an app or an email. It's a good convenient option to use with family members. It's a solid overall photo frame, and has a touchscreen.

Industry observers note that pexar 2K Digital Picture Frame by Lexar for $180: This frame can rotate to be either portrait or landscape mode, and has a little stand that attaches via magnet for either position. It's a fine frame, but the screen isn't as nice as those for a similar price. The Pexar is made by Lexar but uses a third-party app, Frameo, which works fine but has a weirdly Instagram-like uploader that's limited to 10 photos.

Skylight 10-Inch Frame for $190: A previous honorable mention, this frame is still solid. We like other frames better for the price, including the new Skylight Frame 2 (especially with its Snap Frame accessories). There's both a 10-inch version (with only 8 GB of storage) and a 15-inch version (with 16 GB of storage).

Vieunite's Textura Digital Canvas for $754 (USD shown in cart): Beautiful for displaying professional art, this one is bright and high-def enough that you don't lose the integrity of the original painting. It's extremely expensive, though, even if it's cheaper than buying an actual van Gogh.

How Do Digital Photo Frames Work?

Digital photo frames collect your photos, usually through an app but also through email and sometimes text, and display them onto the digital screen. They're created to look like a real frame, but instead show off hundreds or thousands of photos without you needing to reframe anything or print every single picture. Our favorite picks all have an app with storage, so they use Wi-Fi to connect the photos to the frame, but some frames also have physical storage on the device to store and remember the pictures.

What Should You Look For In a Digital Photo Frame?

Here are the top features you should check in a frame:.

What Storage Options Are There on Digital Photo Frames?

All the main frames we recommend use cloud-based storage, so you'll upload your photos to a cloud server for the frame to reach and display them. Aura has unlimited storage for photos, while Nixplay charges $30 a year for unlimited photo storage (along with other features). While both use cloud storage, these are both reputable companies with defined privacy and security practices. Some of the cheaper frames you'll find won't have these processes in place.

Sources indicate that some frames have internal storage that can be expanded with SD cards or even use a USB stick. These options can be more secure, especially if you're moving photos yourself from the computer to the USB or SD card and then connecting it to the frame, but it’s also more work.

Do Smart Displays Work as Digital Photo Frames?

If you already have a smart display, you can set it to cycle through your photo albums when it's idle. The best one for this by far is the Google Nest Max ($230), though the Apple HomeView is another option I'm considering for this guide. It uses Google Photos to pull pictures, so if you're already a Google Photos user, it's an easy transition. But even if you aren't, adding your pictures to Google Photos is much, much easier than using Amazon's uploading tool in the Alexa app if you're using an Echo Show display, though you can also use the Amazon Photos app that works similar to the Google Photos app. You'll use that app for the Alexa Photo Frame I recommend above.

How Does Privacy and Security Come Into Play With Digital Photo Frames?

Sources indicate that you might not think that photos count as sensitive information, compared to a bank account statement or your Social Security number. But it can be devastating to find photos of loved ones used for nefarious or unsavory purposes.

Sources indicate that this is why we prefer frames from reputable companies like Aura and Nixplay over cheaper ones with less clearly defined privacy and security practices. Nixplay offers reasonable security measures, like encrypting your photos during transmission, and Aura offers the option to delete metadata, like the location where a photo was captured. However, both say they may disclose personal information if court-ordered or subpoenaed, and neither provides safety guarantees against hacking.

If you're concerned about security, you can avoid connecting to third-party services, but your most secure option is to just download several photos on a tablet and disable all internet connectivity.

#361. Tech Report: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
